question.text: Chapter 9 states that the startup failure rate in India is approximately __ and __ fail in the first five years. Based on this, how should Mr. Arjun Mehta structure the portfolio of his Cat I Angel Fund 'Himalaya Angels'?

answer.text: 50% failure rate; 30% fail in first 5 years — a 5-company portfolio is enough.
70% failure rate; 60% fail in first 5 years — portfolio of 7 is sufficient.
90% failure rate; 80% fail in first 5 years — minimum 10 companies, expecting 1-2 to give exponential returns that average losses on the rest.
25% failure rate; 15% fail in first 5 years — angels can run concentrated 3-name portfolios.

explanation.text: The Logic: Chapter 9 quotes: 'In India, the failure rate of start-ups is 90%, while 80% of start-ups fail in the first five years. On account of such high risk, angel investors prefer to have a portfolio of minimum 10 companies, out of which they expect 1 or 2 companies to give exponential growth and Net Return on Investments.' The Trap: Options A, B, D all quote lower failure rates and smaller portfolios — these sound intuitively 'reasonable' but contradict the textbook numbers. Test-writers pick option B (70%) as the common-sense distractor. Cross-Exam Context: XIX-C tested this same statistic (all-cat superset). XIX-A tests the portfolio-diversity pitch for client conversations. XV (Research Analyst) doesn't touch start-up failure rates. Manager's Pro-Tip: Angel Fund IC discipline: cap single-investee exposure at ~10% of investible corpus even though the Cat I Angel Fund regulation allows up to 25% (note: Cat I/II general single-investee limit is 25%). A 10-name portfolio at equal weight (10% each) gives both compliance buffer and power-law exposure.
